en: Having prostrated before Śiva, the supreme Lord of Death, hereafter I shall proclaim the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*) to you; listen with concentrated minds.
Here, by the first [verse]:

With their feet, they prostrate before Śiva— the Self-Existent— who is endowed with the auspiciousness (*śivatva*) characterized by being the agent of the knowledge of all objects, who is the cause of the destruction of obstacles, who removes inauspiciousness (*aśiva*), and who bestows auspiciousness upon individual souls (*aṇu*). Having prostrated before that Supreme Śiva, whose specific characteristic exists even in liberated souls (for it is because of this that their state of Śiva-hood is eternally established from the beginning),
yet whose [state] is established from time without beginning.

By the second [verse], having prostrated before his own guru Nidhaneśa— who, through the grace of Śiva, has destroyed all bonds, in whom the vision and action regarding all objects have manifested, and who bestows grace upon all—
he promises, by the third [verse], the knowledge of the subjects contained in all the tantras, initiation, and so forth.
Furthermore, the use of a copulative compound here, *jñānadīkṣe*, is for the purpose of making known the equal importance of both.

For some, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is primary; for one who desires liberation, however, it is both initiation and the exposition [of its meaning]. Furthermore, the statement of the purpose (*prayojana*) stands here before us. Thus, for one who perceives the weightiness of the aphorism (*sūtra*), this presentation of the purpose indicates that, through the current proposition, I too possess the agency in explaining the meaning in certain places, as well as in the division and condensation of the aphorisms.

Furthermore, "abridgment" here does not mean the explanation of the meaning of a previous extensive work by means of a different, shorter work; rather, it refers to the presentation of the other material [of the work] after discarding those explanatory (*arthavāda*) sūtras which merely restate the limbs already mentioned in the *prakṛti* (archetype) that are [already] established by implication in the *vikṛti* (ectype).
[Objection: But in the *Gaurava-sūtra*, only knowledge (*jñāna*) was introduced, whereas here both initiation (*dīkṣā*) and knowledge are introduced. [Response:
It is not only knowledge that was introduced in the *Gaurava-sūtra*; rather, initiation will also follow later on.
He makes it known that initiation (*dīkṣā*) is also included by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) in the opening verse.
By the fourth [verse], having composed his own disciples—such as the Vālakhilyas—who are purified by initiation through the descent of Śiva’s power and who seek knowledge, he establishes them;
for those whose minds are concentrated are capable of discerning the reality of Śiva as it is logically established.

Having thus performed the salutation to the Teacher of the Gods and made his vow, and having composed and established his disciples, such as the Vālakhilyas and others, he recites the Gaurava-sūtra, which summarizes the meaning of the entire Tantra for their understanding, beginning with "Now," and so forth:
"Now, for the sake of liberation from the bonds of karma known as the impurity of the self and māyā, and for the manifestation of Śiva-hood, knowledge proceeds from Śiva. (2)

The word "atha" (now) means that immediately after the state of being oriented toward the exhaustion of the *adhikāra* (office/destiny) which causes the obstruction of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) for those destined for liberation, knowledge proceeds for the sake of grace.
The Self (*ātman*) is all-pervading, eternal, and equal to Śiva;
its impurity (*mala*) is that which obstructs its state of being Śiva.
Bound by that [māyā], he is unable to know or perform his duty or object of knowledge without a means (*upāya*).
For him, who likewise depends upon a means for enjoyment, the bondage called *māyā*—consisting of *kalā* and the other categories—is established.
*Māyā* is the womb of the universe.
The bondage which is its effect is designated by that [name];
for one who is endowed with the means of enjoyment and intends to experience enjoyment, the object of enjoyment is action, which is termed dharma and adharma.

This threefold bondage—consisting of impurity (*mala*) and the rest—is that by which the state of Śiva does not manifest simultaneously in its entirety for the Self when it is joined with it. For the liberation of the Self from this threefold bondage and for the manifestation of its Śiva-nature, knowledge proceeds from Śiva’s desire to bestow grace. That knowledge which proceeds from the bound souls (*paśus*) and from the fetters (*pāśas*) actually produces a further strengthening of those fetters, because it is manifested by them and because it itself has the nature of a fetter. Śiva, however, is distinct from both the bound soul and the fetters; he is the adversary of the fetters and is enriched with all powers.
Therefore, that which proceeds is sufficient and firm for the cessation of the bonds (pāśas).
Of that which possesses obstructed power, it is only a member of the same class that, possessing unobstructed power, manifests its power;
and Śiva is of the same class as the Self.
For one whose Śiva-nature is obstructed, this [state] of unobstructed Śiva-nature initiates its own knowledge for the manifestation of that Śiva-nature; thus it is logical.
That knowledge is twofold: consisting of sound (śabda-rūpa) and consisting of consciousness (avabodha-rūpa).
That which consists of consciousness proceeds toward objects by being mounted upon the form of sound.

"Now, is this not the fruit of initiation? "True; however, it makes known both the goal and the means of the teacher's knowledge. And because he has thus understood the goal and the means, he is able to employ the means for the sake of accomplishing the goal for those who are to be favored.
Furthermore, in all cases, proponents of liberation maintain that knowledge alone is the means for the attainment of liberation;
and that [knowledge] cannot exist without practice."
And even where it is said "only from knowledge," there too the performance of what is to be abandoned and so forth is necessarily required;
or else, since knowledge proceeds from Śiva, knowledge is power (śakti). And that [power] is of two forms: the form of awakening and the form of initiation (dīkṣā).

Just as the ray of the sun, while illuminating objects and also performing burning, does not abandon its nature as light and is thus called "light" despite having both forms, so too Śiva’s power, because it illuminates objects, is called "cognition" (*bodha*). When it effects the removal of the fetters (*pāśas*) and the manifestation of one's own Śiva-nature, it is called "initiation" (*dīkṣā*); even there, it does not abandon its nature as cognition, and therefore it is said to be "cognition" despite possessing both forms.
